name: siril
why: Astronomical image stacking and processing is real science you can run at home on your own telescope data.

brief.what_it_is: Siril is a desktop astronomical image processing program for preprocessing and processing telescope images. It takes raw camera frames, FITS files, and SER video sequences, applies calibration with bias, dark and flat master frames, registers and stacks many frames into one image, then offers enhancement tools such as colour calibration, deconvolution and histogram stretching. It also has science tools for star brightness variation and astrometry. It ships as a GUI app with a companion command-line binary, siril-cli. The homepage describes it as 'an astronomical image processing tool'.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames the job as improving signal-to-noise ratio by combining many registered frames, and removing unwanted signal and pattern from raw images in a calibration step. It presents itself as a complete workflow from raw data to publishable image, usable manually or through scripts.
brief.how_it_works: Preprocessing writes out a new file for each step, using the SER or FITS-cube formats to keep this cheap. Stacking methods run in parallel across all cores, and registration can align on all stars, one star, or the nebulosity, which the site says helps with faint stars. Outlier rejection during stacking further reduces noise.
brief.install_notes: Downloads are offered per platform from the homepage: Linux AppImage, a third-party Flathub Flatpak (flagged with a warning), Windows 64-bit UCRT64 installer and Portable UCRT64 build, and macOS Intel and Apple Silicon builds. The Windows MINGW64 builds are marked deprecated. The README pages I reached did not describe any runtime, account, or configuration steps, and no first-run instructions were visible. The homepage asks users who publish work with Siril to cite the JOSS paper.
brief.standout: It processes SER video natively, so lucky-imaging workflows with tens of thousands of frames are practical, and the site claims 10,000 images can be processed in about the time it takes to drink a coffee. The project is open source under GPLv3 and is also published as a journal article in the Journal of Open Source Software.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists version 1.4.4 released June 17, 2026, and recent news posts run through October 17, 2026. The GitLab project page shows GPLv3 licensing and a CHANGELOG and CONTRIBUTING file, though I did not read those.
brief.caveats: The Linux Flatpak is third-party and the homepage says there are known issues with the current version, pointing to the bug tracker. Windows MINGW64 builds are deprecated. The GitLab page I reached showed only a short project blurb, not a full README, so I could not verify installation steps or the command-line interface. No command examples appeared on the homepage. The claims about speed and frame counts are the project's own marketing and I could not benchmark them.
